subject: Clarify default storage scope and erasure playbook for streaming vs final outputs
messages:
From: Sarah Holt <sarah.holt@evergrovehealth.com>
To: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.ai>
Cc: Evergrove Security <security@evergrovehealth.com>
Date: 2026-09-03T09:12:00Z
Subject: Questions on what Redwood keeps by default (streaming fragments vs final outputs)

Hi Marissa,

Thanks for the demo yesterday — Evergrove likes the low-latency routing. Before we move the pilot forward, our security/compliance team has a few targeted questions on default retention semantics so we can complete our internal risk assessment. These are specific to hosted Redwood API behavior (we're not asking about Private/Dedicated yet):

1) For streaming responses (token-by-token streaming and partial fragments), does Redwood persist the streaming fragments by default or are they transient until the final output is produced? If fragments are persisted, for how long?

2) For completed requests (full prompt + final model output), what is the default retention window? Please call out any differences for: plain text prompts, binary attachments referenced in requests, and structured outputs (JSON).

3) Do prompt derivatives (summaries, embeddings, reranking artifacts) created by Redwood get retained by default? If so, under what retention classes?

4) What's the standard customer-initiated deletion process? We need to understand how Evergrove can request erasure and what proof/redaction evidence Redwood provides (timelines and export of deletion logs).

I've attached our short security questionnaire (security-questionnaire.pdf). If possible, could you provide a short summary and an export template to share with our legal folks?

Appreciate a concise response we can include in our compliance package.

Best,
Sarah
Sarah Holt
Director, Cloud Security
Evergrove Health

From: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.ai>
To: Sarah Holt <sarah.holt@evergrovehealth.com>
Cc: Evergrove Security <security@evergrovehealth.com>, Kimberly Park <kimberly_park@redwood.ai>, Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.ai>
Date: 2026-09-03T12:45:00Z
Subject: Re: Questions on what Redwood keeps by default (streaming fragments vs final outputs)

Hi Sarah — thanks for the clear list. Looping in Kimberly (policy + compliance) and Karthik (runtime) so you get both the policy and the technical picture. High-level summary below, followed by proposed next steps and requested attachments. We'll produce a short one-page summary you can slot into Evergrove's package.

High-level answers (summary):
- Streaming fragments: treated as transient buffering by default and not indexed for long-term retention; they are kept only for the duration of the request processing pipeline plus a short buffering window for reliability.
- Completed request + final outputs: retained by default for a standard 30-day review window (hosts only), after which they are automatically expired unless the customer has configured "store_outputs" or has a Dedicated/Private contract with different terms.
- Derivatives (embeddings/summaries): by default, derivatives are NOT stored unless explicitly enabled via the API or by product features (e.g., persistent embeddings for semantic search).
- Deletion workflow: customer requests go through Support with org id + request id. Standard turnaround: 48–72 hours to initiate erasure, full confirmation and deletion report within 7–10 business days for hosted accounts. We will attach the deletion evidence template.

Attachments: redwood-retention-summary.pdf (short explainer), and we will add a deletion-evidence template once Karthik confirms the technical details below.

Next steps: Karthik, can you confirm the exact buffering window we expose for streamed fragments and whether anything from the streaming buffer is written to persistent logs in the hosted path? Also, can you confirm the default retention clock start (from request timestamp or from finalization time)?

Sarah/Security team — if the above looks OK, we can schedule a 30-min tech call to walk through examples and produce a brief, signed evidence report.

Thanks,
Marissa
Marissa Cole
Senior Account Executive, Redwood Inference
From: Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.ai>
To: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.ai>, Kimberly Park <kimberly_park@redwood.ai>, Sarah Holt <sarah.holt@evergrovehealth.com>
Cc: Evergrove Security <security@evergrovehealth.com>
Date: 2026-09-03T15:02:00Z
Subject: Re: Questions on what Redwood keeps by default (streaming fragments vs final outputs)

Hi all — quick technical clarifications to back Marissa's summary. I'll keep this tight and prescriptive so you can paste into your compliance doc.

1) Streaming fragments (token-by-token buffer):
- Default behavior (hosted API): streaming fragments are held in ephemeral in-memory buffers and a short-lived write-ahead buffer for reliability. That write-ahead buffer is rotated and retained for 30 minutes by default to support reconnection and immediate diagnostics. Nothing from streaming fragments is indexed into long-term logs unless the request completes with a flag that triggers storage (e.g., "store_outputs" or customer-configured audit mode).

2) Completed request + final outputs:
- Default retention window (hosted): 30 days from the request completion timestamp. During this 30-day window we retain the raw request (prompt), metadata (client/org id, model, route), and the final output.
- Attachments: binary attachments referenced in the request are stored in object storage tied to the request record and follow the same 30-day default retention unless configured otherwise at account level.
- Structured outputs (JSON): stored as part of the request record and also included in export bundles.

3) Prompt derivatives (embeddings, summaries, reranks):
- Default: derivatives are NOT persisted by default. If derivatives are generated by product features (e.g., customer-enabled embeddings), they are stored under a separate retention class with a 180-day default TTL unless the customer explicitly sets a different lifecycle policy.

4) Deletion / erasure process and evidence:
- Request: customer submits a support request at support.redwood.ai with org id + CN/contract id.
- Kickoff: Support acknowledges within 24 business hours and creates an internal erasure job.
- Execution: Hosted accounts: deletion job purges request records and associated object storage within 48–72 hours after job start. We then run a verification sweep to ensure tombstoning of any derived caches; final confirmation report is generated within 7 business days.
- Evidence: we provide a PDF report that includes: list of deleted request IDs, timestamps of deletion steps, confirmation checks, and a signed statement of completion. For customers needing attestation, we can include a redacted export of deletion logs.

Notes / edge cases:
- Audit hold: If an account has an active legal hold or is part of a support investigation, automated deletion is blocked until the hold is cleared; in that case we provide a formal hold notice and next-step timeline.
- Private/Dedicated: customers on Dedicated/private deployments can set custom TTLs and may opt for automated shorter or longer retention; those contracts supersede hosted defaults.

I'll attach the internal deletion-evidence template and will coordinate with Compliance for the final PDF.

-Karthik
Karthik Iyer
Principal Infra Engineer, Redwood Inference

If you can provide those two items and the one-page summary Marissa referenced, we should be able to close our internal review this week. I'd also like an export template for deletion evidence (we've attached POC_Evidence_Req.xlsx with fields we expect).
